overview.title: LossHistory output (fig. 7.5) and why TensorBoard (7.3.4)
overview.section: 7.3 Using built-in training and evaluation loops
overview.main_topic: Finishing the LossHistory test-drive, its per-batch loss plot, and the motivation for TensorBoard: the idea-experiment-results loop of progress
overview.central_idea: Passing callbacks=[LossHistory()] to fit() produces per-epoch plots of per-batch training loss (figure 7.5). Section 7.3.4 then argues that progress is an iterative loop - idea, experiment, results - and that, while Keras and GPUs speed up the first two arcs, TensorBoard is the tool for processing results.
overview.importance: It closes the custom-callback example with its visible output and frames TensorBoard not as a gadget but as a way to shorten the research iteration loop.

summary:
The page first finishes the test-drive started on p.235. The `model.fit(` call continues with `train_images`, `train_labels`, `epochs=10`, `callbacks=[LossHistory()]` and `validation_data=(val_images, val_labels)`. The authors say "We get plots that look like figure 7.5".

**Figure 7.5**, "The output of our custom history-plotting callback", is one of the saved plots: the x-axis is labelled `Batch (epoch 0)` and runs to about 1,600 batches, the y-axis is `Loss`, and the legend reads "Training loss for each batch". The loss starts near 2.3, falls steeply below 1.0 within the first ~100 batches, and then decreases slowly to roughly 0.3 by the end of the first epoch.

**Section 7.3.4, Monitoring and visualization with TensorBoard**, opens with a broader argument. Good research and good models need "rich, frequent feedback" about what's going on inside the model; that is the point of experiments. Progress is a **loop**: start with an idea, express it as an experiment that tries to validate or invalidate it, run the experiment, process the information it generates, and let that inspire the next idea. The more iterations you can run, the more refined and powerful your ideas become. **Figure 7.6**, "The loop of progress", shows Idea -> Experiment (via the deep learning framework, Keras) -> Results (via GPUs, TPUs) -> back to Idea (via the visualization framework, TensorBoard). Keras minimises the time from idea to experiment, and fast GPUs the time from experiment to result; for processing the results, "That's where TensorBoard comes in". What TensorBoard actually offers is described on p.237.

paragraphs.excerpt: We get plots that look like figure 7.5.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Figure 7.5 shows one of the saved plots: per-batch training loss during epoch 0, starting around 2.3 and decaying to about 0.3 over roughly 1,600 batches.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The shape - a steep initial drop and a long slow tail - is typical of training a classifier from scratch: early steps fix gross errors (e.g. learning class frequencies and obvious strokes), later steps make fine refinements. The starting value of about 2.3 matches ln(10) ≈ 2.303, the crossentropy of a model that assigns equal probability to all 10 digit classes. (Beyond the book.)
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Reading such a plot lets you sanity-check training: a starting loss far from ln(num_classes) suggests an initialisation or label problem; a curve that doesn't fall suggests a learning-rate or data problem.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: roughly 1,560 batches per epoch is consistent with about 50,000 training samples at Keras's default batch size of 32 (50,000/32 ≈ 1,563). The smoothness is partly because batch-level 'loss' in logs is a running mean over the epoch so far.

paragraphs.excerpt: To do good research or develop good models, you need rich, frequent feedback
paragraphs.what_it_says: Experiments exist to get as much information as possible about how well a model performs. Progress is an iterative loop of idea -> experiment -> processing results -> next idea; more iterations make ideas more refined and powerful. Keras shortens idea-to-experiment, fast GPUs shorten experiment-to-result, and TensorBoard addresses processing the results.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors measure research productivity by loop iteration speed. Each tool in figure 7.6 accelerates one arc; a slow arc (e.g. squinting at console logs) bottlenecks the whole loop.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It motivates investing in monitoring: better visibility into training is as valuable as faster hardware because it speeds up the step that generates the next idea.

concepts.name: Loop of progress
concepts.definition: The iterative cycle idea -> experiment -> results -> new idea (figure 7.6).
concepts.intuition: Like a scientist's hypothesis-test cycle: the faster you go around it, the faster you learn.

concepts.name: TensorBoard
concepts.definition: A visualization framework for processing experiment results, introduced here and described on p.237.
concepts.intuition: The dashboard of the training run.
concepts.technical: Reads log files written during training (via a Keras callback, p.237).
concepts.significance: Closes the results->idea arc of the loop.

math.title: Expected initial crossentropy for 10 equiprobable classes
math.source_text: (not printed; explains the starting value ~2.3 in figure 7.5)
math.operations: Natural logarithm of the uniform probability 1/K assigned to the true class.
math.purpose: Sanity check for the first point of the per-batch loss curve.
math.interpretation: A freshly initialised classifier outputs roughly uniform softmax probabilities, so its crossentropy is about log K.
math.intuition: Knowing nothing, the model gives each digit a 10% chance; -ln(0.1) ≈ 2.3.
math.numerical_example: $-\ln(0.1) = 2.3026$; figure 7.5's first value is just under 2.3. After training, a loss of 0.3 corresponds to an average true-class probability around $e^{-0.3}\approx 0.74$ (geometric mean).

deeper.title: Reading figure 7.5 as a diagnostic
deeper.body:
- **Start (~2.3)**: matches $\ln 10$, so the network starts out as an unbiased 10-way guesser - initialisation and labels look sane.
- **Steep drop (first ~100 batches)**: Adam quickly learns the easy structure.
- **Long tail (to ~0.3)**: slower refinement. Within one epoch, it has not plateaued, so more epochs are worthwhile.
- **What the plot can't tell you**: overfitting. It shows training loss only; you need validation curves (e.g. in TensorBoard, p.237) for that.

(Beyond the book.)

deeper.title: The loop of progress as a lab notebook
deeper.body: Think of a chemist: hypothesis (idea), bench work (experiment, sped up by good equipment = Keras + GPUs), and analysis of the readings (results, sped up by good instruments = TensorBoard). A lab with fast reactions but no way to read results still learns slowly.

questions.question: In figure 7.6, which arc of the loop does TensorBoard accelerate?
questions.explanation: The arc from Results to Idea is labelled 'Visualization framework: TensorBoard'. Keras labels Idea->Experiment and GPUs/TPUs label Experiment->Results.

questions.question: Why does the loss in figure 7.5 start near 2.3? Compute the expected value.
questions.answer: An untrained 10-class softmax gives ≈0.1 to the true class; crossentropy = -ln(0.1) = ln 10 ≈ 2.303.
questions.explanation: Sparse categorical crossentropy is -log p(true class); uniform predictions give log K.

questions.question: How many plot files does the test-drive fit() call produce, and how are they named?
questions.answer: Ten: plot_at_epoch_0 through plot_at_epoch_9, one per epoch.
questions.explanation: epochs=10 and LossHistory saves f"plot_at_epoch_{epoch}" in on_epoch_end.

questions.question: According to the authors, why does the number of iterations of the idea-experiment-results loop matter?
questions.answer: Each iteration processes information that inspires the next idea; the more iterations you run, the more refined and powerful your ideas become.
